definition.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

facts.text: Its main goal is a larger total yield by using resources a single crop would leave unused.
Crops are paired to avoid competing, such as deep-rooted with shallow-rooted, or tall with shade-tolerant.
In low-input systems it can give higher yields for the same input, or steadier yields with less.
A companion crop can support plants prone to falling over, or supply nutrients.
Results vary: a 2008 review found predators rose in only 53% of studies and yields in only 32%.
Crop rotation differs because its crops grow in separate seasons.

definition.text: Sowing a second crop while the first is still growing, so the first is harvested to make room for the second.

facts.text: Related temporal intercropping pairs a fast-growing crop with a slow one, harvesting the fast crop first, and can out-yield either alone.

definition.text: Pest control that pairs an attractive trap crop pulling pests in with a repellent crop pushing them away from the main crop.

facts.text: In a 2006 review of 100 trap crops, only 10 succeeded commercially, all with added measures to stop insects returning to the main crop.

definition.text: Growing crops between rows of nitrogen-fixing Inga trees, whose pruned leaves form a thick mulch.

facts.text: It lets land be farmed repeatedly, offering an alternative to destructive slash-and-burn cultivation.
Mike Hands developed and trialled it in Costa Rica in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

title: No-till farming

definition.text: Growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

facts.text: It reduces erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils, and can improve water infiltration, organic matter and nutrient cycling.
Worldwide area grew from about 45 million ha in 1999 to 111 million ha in 2009.
In Argentina it cut erosion losses by 80% and costs by more than 50%; in Paraguay net farm incomes rose 77%.
Fewer machinery passes lower fuel and labour costs.
Without tillage to remove weeds, farmers commonly use herbicides such as glyphosate, increasing herbicide use.
Nitrogen tied up in residue can mean higher fertilizer rates, and cold, wet spring soil can delay planting.
Whether it increases soil carbon is debated; some studies suspect flawed testing or losses deeper in the soil.
England's DEFRA pays farmers £73 per hectare to convert.

contested_note: Sources debate whether the extra soil carbon reported under no-till is real or an artefact of testing methods.

definition.text: A group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled.

facts.text: No-till and strip tillage are both forms of it, but no-till is not the same thing.
Tillage, mechanically stirring the soil, has been used since at least 3000 B.C.
By 2014 more than 75% of Canadian Prairie cropland had adopted it.
